[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Deep Learning Tutorial: Loss Functions in Regression, Classification, and Ranking"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Loss functions are the mathematical compass of any deep learning model. They quantify how well a model's predictions align with the ground truth labels. Minimizing this loss through gradient descent drives the learning process. This tutorial covers the fundamental loss functions used across three core machine learning tasks: Regression, Classification, and Ranking."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Regression Loss Functions"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Regression tasks involve predicting continuous numerical values. The choice of loss function dictates how the model penalizes large errors versus small errors."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Mean Squared Error (MSE / L2 Loss): Computes the average squared difference between estimated values and actual value. It severely penalizes large errors due to the squaring operation."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Mean Absolute Error (MAE / L1 Loss): Computes the average absolute difference. It is more robust to outliers than MSE, but its gradient is constant, which can hinder convergence near the minimum."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Huber Loss: Acts as a hybrid, behaving like MSE when the error is small and like MAE when the error is large, blending robustness and smoothness."},{"order":8,"type":"code","text":"import torch
import torch.nn as nn

# Sample predictions and targets
y_pred = torch.tensor([2.5, 0.0, 2.1], requires_grad=True)
y_true = torch.tensor([3.0, -0.5, 2.0])

# Define regression losses
mse_loss = nn.MSELoss()
mae_loss = nn.L1Loss()
huber_loss = nn.HuberLoss(delta=1.0)

print('MSE:', mse_loss(y_pred, y_true).item())
print('MAE:', mae_loss(y_pred, y_true).item())
print('Huber:', huber_loss(y_pred, y_true).item())"},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Classification Loss Functions"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"Classification tasks predict discrete class labels. Deep learning models typically output raw scores called logits, which are then mapped to probabilities."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE): Used for binary classification (0 or 1). It measures the performance of a model whose output is a probability value between 0 and 1."},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Categorical Cross-Entropy: Used for multi-class classification where targets are one-hot encoded vectors."},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Sparse Categorical Cross-Entropy: Similar to categorical cross-entropy, but targets are provided as integer class indices, saving memory."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"# Binary Cross Entropy
bce_loss = nn.BCELoss()
preds_binary = torch.tensor([0.9, 0.1, 0.8])
targets_binary = torch.tensor([1.0, 0.0, 1.0])
print('BCE Loss:', bce_loss(preds_binary, targets_binary).item())

# Cross Entropy (combines LogSoftmax and NLLLoss in PyTorch)
ce_loss = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
logits = torch.tensor([[2.0, 1.0, 0.1], [0.5, 2.5, 0.3]])
classes = torch.tensor([0, 1])
print('Cross Entropy Loss:', ce_loss(logits, classes).item())"},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Ranking Loss Functions"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"Ranking tasks are common in recommendation systems, search engines, and metric learning. Instead of absolute values or classes, ranking losses optimize the relative order of items."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Margin Ranking Loss: Computes loss given input tensors x1, x2 and a label tensor y (containing 1 or -1). If y=1, it expects x1 to be ranked higher than x2 (i.e., x1 > x2 + margin)."},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Triplet Loss: Commonly used in face recognition and metric learning. It takes an anchor, a positive (same class), and a negative (different class) sample, ensuring the anchor is closer to the positive than to the negative by a margin."},{"order":19,"type":"code","text":"# Margin Ranking Loss
ranking_loss = nn.MarginRankingLoss(margin=1.0)
x1 = torch.tensor([2.5, 1.0])
x2 = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0])
y = torch.tensor([1, -1])
print('Margin Ranking Loss:', ranking_loss(x1, x2, y).item())

# Triplet Margin Loss
triplet_loss = nn.TripletMarginLoss(margin=1.0, p=2.0)
anchor = torch.tensor([[0.1, 0.2], [0.5, 0.5]])
positive = torch.tensor([[0.2, 0.2], [0.6, 0.4]])
negative = torch.tensor([[0.9, 0.8], [0.1, 0.9]])
print('Triplet Loss:', triplet_loss(anchor, positive, negative).item())"},{"order":20,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":21,"type":"paragraph","text":"Selecting the correct loss function is vital for deep learning success. Use regression losses (MSE, MAE, Huber) for continuous targets, cross-entropy variants for probabilistic class predictions, and ranking/triplet losses when relative ordering or metric distance is the primary objective."}]
